extracted.intended_audience: U.S. patent examiners, patent practitioners, and attorneys involved in patent prosecution
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating patent claims for obviousness, reasonable expectation of success, claim interpretation, and related claim-limitations issues under 35 U.S.C. §§102, 103, and 112 (MPEP guidance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching away / weight of prior-art statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether statements in a prior art reference that limit the function or capability of a prior art device constitute teaching away from combining that reference with others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give fair consideration to statements that limit function/capability, but note that simplicity of the prior art is rarely a characteristic that weighs against obviousness of a more complicated device with added function. Case examples: In re Dance (claimed catheter obvious despite primary reference stressing simplicity), Allied Erecting v. Genesis Attachments (advantages/disadvantages do not necessarily obviate motivation to combine). If the prior art teaches that a proposed modification would render a process inoperable or produce undesirable properties, that may support teaching away (see cited cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposed modification must not change principle of operation
rubrics_metrics.description: If the proposed modification or combination of prior art would change the principle of operation of the prior art invention being modified, the references do not supply sufficient teachings to render the claims prima facie obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rejections based on combinations that would require a fundamental redesign or change in the basic principle of operation are improper. Example: In re Ratti (reversal where primary reference required rigidity but claimed invention required resiliency; suggested combination would change basic operating principle). Examiners should assess whether combination requires substantial reconstruction or alteration of the reference's operating principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable expectation of success required for obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Where there is reason to modify or combine prior art to achieve the claimed invention, a prima facie obviousness rejection also requires a reasonable expectation (likelihood) of success in making the modification or combination to meet the claim limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expectation of success refers to the likelihood that combining/modifying prior art would achieve the claimed invention. It may be shown implicitly via the prior art teachings or explicitly; depending on circumstances implicit showing may be insufficient. Examiners should include, explicitly or implicitly, an indication of reasonable expectation of success in an obviousness rejection. Case examples: Elekta Ltd. v. ZAP Surgical Sys., Intelligent Bio‑Sys. v. Illumina, In re Merck & Co., Ex parte Blanc. Note: conclusive proof of efficacy is not required and absolute predictability is not required (OSI Pharm. v. Apotex; Acorda v. Roxane; PharmaStem; Pfizer v. Apotex). Preamble or other claim limitations relevant to intended purpose may be relevant to the reasonable expectation analysis (Eli Lilly v. Teva).

rubrics_metrics.name: Some degree of predictability is required; evidence of unpredictability can rebut obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness does not require absolute predictability, but at least some degree of predictability is required; evidence that there was no reasonable expectation of success may support nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants may present evidence (e.g., experimental failures, high failure rates, lack of reliable indicators) showing that the only reasonable expectation at the time was failure. Case examples: In re Rinehart (no reasonable expectation of successful scale-up), OSI Pharm. v. Apotex (high failure rate in unpredictable art), Amgen v. Chugai (biotechnology unpredictability), In re O'Farrell (detailed enabling methodology in reference supported obviousness). Examiners should evaluate the predictability of the art and the weight of evidence regarding expected success at the relevant time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictability assessed at the relevant time
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether an art is predictable or whether a proposed modification/combination had a reasonable expectation of success is judged at the relevant time (time of the invention for pre‑AIA; before the effective filing date for AIA/FITF applications).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine predictability and expectation of success based on knowledge available at the relevant time. Example: Ex parte Erlich (motivation and reasonable expectation assessed as of the time the invention was made). Use the appropriate temporal standard depending on whether the application is pre‑AIA or subject to AIA.

rubrics_metrics.name: All claim limitations must be considered in obviousness analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners must consider every limiting term in a claim when determining patentability over the prior art; 'All words in a claim must be considered in judging the patentability of that claim against the prior art.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The subject matter of the properly construed claim (broadest reasonable interpretation) must be examined. Grammar and ordinary meaning as understood by one of ordinary skill often dictate whether language is limiting. If an independent claim is nonobvious under 35 U.S.C. 103, generally dependent claims are nonobvious, unless dependency is improper or dependent claim has a later effective filing date. See In re Wilson, In re Gulack, Axonics v. Medtronic, In re Fine. Examiners should avoid improperly narrowing claim scope to preferred embodiments (Axonics example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Indefinite claim limitations must be considered (cannot be disregarded)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim limitation considered indefinite cannot be disregarded; if a claim has more than one reasonable interpretation and at least one renders the claim unpatentable over the prior art, reject the claim as indefinite and, when appropriate, reject over the prior art based on the interpretation that renders the prior art applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rejecting on both indefiniteness (35 U.S.C. 112(b)) and prior art grounds when appropriate avoids piecemeal review. However, examiners must not base prior art rejections on speculative or unreasonable claim interpretations; substantial speculation is improper (see In re Steele, In re Wilson, Ex parte Ionescu). See MPEP § 2175 and § 2111 for proper claim interpretation guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations lacking support in the original specification must still be considered
rubrics_metrics.description: When evaluating obviousness, all claim limitations must be considered, including limitations that do not find support in the specification as originally filed (i.e., new matter or negative limitations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not ignore negative limitations or terms absent from the specification when assessing patentability over the prior art. Example: Ex parte Grasselli (negative exclusions not in original specification were still properly considered). 'All words in a claim must be considered' (In re Miller, quoting In re Wilson).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim language types that may raise questions about limiting effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain kinds of claim language may raise questions about whether they limit claim scope (this list is not exhaustive): preambles, clauses like 'adapted to', 'adapted for', 'wherein', 'whereby', contingent limitations, printed matter, and functional language associated with a claim term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should analyze whether such language functions as a claim limitation in the specific factual context. See MPEP §§2111.01–2111.05 for discussion of preambles, transitional phrases, contingent limitations, printed matter, and functional language. Proper claim interpretation determines whether the prior art teaches the limitation.
